title: When the Letter Falls
premise: In the winter of 1899, during a colonial border war, battlefield nurse Theo Nakamura secretly records in his ledger the names of soldiers erased from official reports—men whose deaths would embarrass their commanders. When a dying courier presses a sealed letter into his hands, Theo discovers it names the family of his closest friend as conspirators in a fabricated treason plot designed to cover an officer's embezzlement. With three military checkpoints between him and the governor-general's office, and the century turning in eleven days, Theo must smuggle the letter and his ledger through occupied territory, aided by a deserter, a widow who runs a river ferry, and the very family the letter condemns. At the final checkpoint he is recognized and arrested, but the ledger's copies—already distributed among the families of the erased dead—force a public inquiry that clears the family on New Year's Day, though Theo pays for justice with his position, his anonymity, and nearly his life.
about_author: Noor Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing colonial-era military correspondence in Cape Town and London. Fascinated by the small hands that history overlooks, she writes fiction about the people who kept the records no one was meant to read.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Cot
chapters.summary: Theo Nakamura, POV. In a muddy field hospital, Theo tends the wounded by day and records omitted names in a hidden ledger by night—a habit born when his own brother's death went unrecorded. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: he cannot stop the war, but he can refuse to let it erase people.

chapters.title: Names That Were Never There
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. A supply clerk notices discrepancies between Theo's tallies and official reports and warns him to burn the ledger. Theo refuses but begins copying pages and hiding them separately. The beat is mounting unease—the first hint that someone powerful benefits from the missing names.

chapters.title: A Courier at the Wire
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. During a night shelling, a wounded civilian courier crawls into the aid station clutching a sealed letter addressed to the governor-general. Dying, he makes Theo swear to deliver it. The beat is reluctant duty: Theo wants no part of politics, but a promise is a promise.

chapters.title: What the Wax Conceals
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Unable to resist, Theo steams the letter open and finds it names the Okonkwo family—traders who sheltered him once—as parties to a treason plot he suspects is fabricated to bury an officer's theft. The beat is horror: delivering the letter destroys innocents; destroying it makes him a criminal.

chapters.title: The House on Ferry Lane
chapters.summary: Adaeze Okonkwo, POV. Adaeze runs her late husband's river ferry and reads the letter over Theo's objections. She recognizes the officer's signature as forged—her father taught penmanship. The beat is fierce clarity: they will not run; they will answer the lie with evidence.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints, Eleven Days
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo maps the route to the capital: the bridge checkpoint, the rail yard, and the fort gate, each more dangerous than the last. New Year's honors list deadline looms—the plot must be buried before then. The beat is cold arithmetic of time and risk.

chapters.title: The Deserter Who Knew the Bridge
chapters.summary: Corporal Elias Voss, POV. A deserter caught stealing morphine bargains his knowledge of the bridge checkpoint's shift rotations in exchange for passage out. Theo distrusts him but needs him. The beat is uneasy alliance—two men using each other toward different salvations.

chapters.title: Ledger Pages as Currency
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo realizes his ledger itself is leverage: families of the erased dead will shelter him if he gives them proof. He begins distributing copied pages through Adaeze's ferry network. The beat is transformation—from hiding the truth to weaponizing it.

chapters.title: First Crossing
chapters.summary: Theo and Voss, alternating POV. The bridge crossing succeeds only because a grieving mother among the guards recognizes her son's name in the ledger and looks away. The beat is fragile grace: justice outside the law depends on ordinary mercy.

chapters.title: The Officer Who Signed Twice
chapters.summary: Major Calloway, POV. The antagonist inspects the courier's death report, realizes the letter may have survived, and orders Theo's aid station searched. The beat is dread from the other side: Calloway is not a monster but a tired man protecting a career built on one forgery.

chapters.title: Ashes in the Aid Tent
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Soldiers ransack the hospital; Theo's original ledger is burned before his eyes while he stands at attention. Only the distributed copies survive. The beat is grief and resolve fused—he has lost the archive but gained witnesses.

chapters.title: Ferry at Moonrise
chapters.summary: Adaeze, POV. Adaeze ferries Theo and the letter downriver by night, evading a patrol boat, while confessing her fear that saving her family will cost Theo everything. The beat is intimacy under pressure—an almost-love neither names.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Rail Yard
chapters.summary: Voss, POV. Cornered by Calloway's men, Voss trades Theo's route for amnesty and leads them to the rail yard. The beat is bitter inevitability: Voss never promised loyalty, only information—and even that had a price.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo slips past the rail yard hidden in a coffin bound for the capital, sharing darkness with a dead soldier whose name he adds to the ledger by matchlight. The beat is claustrophobic communion with death—the book's thematic heart.

chapters.title: The Family Condemned
chapters.summary: Adaeze, POV. Back home, the Okonkwos are arrested on the letter's authority; Adaeze escapes with her younger brother and goes underground with the ferry network. The beat is fury sharpened into purpose—the condemned become the couriers.

chapters.title: Calloway's Offer
chapters.summary: Calloway and Theo, POV. Captured briefly, Theo is offered freedom and reinstatement if he surrenders the letter and testifies that the Okonkwos are guilty. The beat is temptation made human: Calloway genuinely believes order matters more than truth.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo escapes with help from the widow of an erased soldier, choosing certain ruin over complicity. He mails half the ledger to a newspaper editor and keeps the letter for the governor-general himself. The beat is the point of no return, crossed without hesitation.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Fort Gate
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. On New Year's Eve, Theo walks openly to the fort gate carrying the letter in plain sight, betting that Calloway dare not shoot a man surrendering documents publicly. Guards hesitate; crowds gather—families holding ledger pages. The beat is courage as spectacle.

chapters.title: Century's End
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. Calloway orders Theo seized anyway; in the scuffle the letter is read aloud by a printer's apprentice from the crowd, and the crowd repeats it line by line until the garrison commander must receive it formally. The beat is climax: truth spoken in chorus cannot be unspoken.

chapters.title: The Inquiry Opens
chapters.summary: Theo, imprisoned, POV. From his cell Theo watches the machinery turn: handwriting experts confirm the forgery, the newspaper prints the ledger excerpts, and the Okonkwo family is released pending trial. The beat is exhausted hope—justice arriving slowly, imperfectly, but arriving.

chapters.title: New Year's Day
chapters.summary: Adaeze, POV. The charges are quashed; Calloway resigns rather than face court-martial. Adaeze secures Theo's release by testifying to his character, and the two stand at the ferry landing as church bells ring in 1900. The beat is quiet triumph and tender beginning.

chapters.title: A Ledger With Room Left
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Epilogue: Theo declines reinstatement, instead opening a small record office where families can register their own dead—no officer's permission required. The last page of his old ledger holds one new name: the courier who started it all. The beat is resolution as vocation: memory kept by willing hands.
